1.fact: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, making up about 75 percent of all normal matter by mass.

2.fact: Helium was first spotted in the Sun's light during an 1868 solar eclipse, decades before anyone found it on Earth.

3.fact: Lithium is the least dense of all metals, so light that it can float on water.

4.fact: Beryllium lets X-rays pass through it so easily that it is used for the windows of X-ray tubes.

5.fact: Boron gives a bright green colour to flames, so it is used in green flares and fireworks.

6.fact: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; only the way the atoms bond makes one the hardest natural material and the other soft enough for pencils.

7.fact: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air you breathe.

8.fact: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and so magnetic that it can hang as a bridge between the poles of a powerful magnet.

9.fact: Fluorine reacts with every other element except the lightest noble gases, yet fluoride made from it is added to toothpaste to fight tooth decay.

10.fact: Neon glows a vivid reddish orange in a glass tube with electricity running through it, the colour that made neon signs famous.

11.fact: Sodium is a metal soft enough to cut with a knife, and it reacts violently with water.

12.fact: Burning magnesium gives off a brilliant white light, which is why early photographers used magnesium powder for flash.

13.fact: Before industrial production began in 1856, aluminium was so hard to make that it cost more than gold.

14.fact: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, after oxygen.

15.fact: Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, who was boiling down urine in search of the philosopher's stone.

16.fact: Sulfur was known in ancient times as brimstone, and Homer's Iliad and Odyssey both mention its smell after lightning strikes.

17.fact: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas, and its name comes from the Greek word chloros, meaning pale green.

18.fact: Argon makes up almost 1 percent of Earth's atmosphere, about 23 times as much as carbon dioxide.

19.fact: Your nerves and muscles need potassium to work, and bananas are a well-known source of it.

20.fact: Calcium is the most abundant metal in the human body, and the fifth most abundant element in it.

21.fact: Mendeleev predicted scandium in 1869, calling it ekaboron, ten years before it was discovered in 1879.

22.fact: Titanium has the highest strength-to-density ratio of any metal, so it is used in jet engines and spacecraft.

23.fact: Vanadium is named after Vanadís, a name of the Norse goddess Freyja, because its compounds come in so many beautiful colours.

24.fact: Traces of chromium give rubies their red colour and emeralds their green.

25.fact: Lumps called manganese nodules, often about the size of a potato, lie scattered across large areas of the deep ocean floor.

26.fact: Iron is the most common element on Earth by mass, and much of it lies in the planet's core.

27.fact: Cobalt is named after kobolds, goblins that German miners blamed for ores that gave off poisonous fumes and no useful metal.

28.fact: The US five-cent coin is called a nickel, but it is three quarters copper and only one quarter nickel.

29.fact: Copper slowly turns green as it weathers, which is why the Statue of Liberty is green instead of copper-coloured.

30.fact: A thin coat of zinc stops steel from rusting, a process called galvanizing.

31.fact: Gallium melts at about 30 °C, so a piece of it can melt in your hand.

32.fact: Mendeleev predicted germanium in 1869, calling it ekasilicon, 17 years before Clemens Winkler found it in 1886.

33.fact: At normal air pressure, arsenic does not melt: it turns straight from a solid into a gas.

34.fact: Selenium conducts electricity better in light than in the dark, which made it useful in early light meters and photocopiers.

35.fact: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury.

36.fact: From 1960 to 1983 the length of a metre was officially defined by the light given off by krypton atoms.

37.fact: Rubidium was discovered in 1861 from deep red lines in its spectrum, and its name comes from the Latin for deep red.

38.fact: Strontium compounds give fireworks and road flares their bright red colour.

39.fact: Yttrium is named after Ytterby, a Swedish village where a heavy black rock found in an old quarry in 1787 led to its discovery.

40.fact: Zirconium hardly absorbs neutrons, so it is used to wrap the fuel rods inside nuclear reactors.

41.fact: Niobium is named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth, because it is so similar to tantalum.

42.fact: Bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into food for plants rely on enzymes that contain molybdenum.

43.fact: Technetium, made in 1937, was the first mostly artificial element, and its name comes from the Greek technetos, meaning artificial.

44.fact: Ruthenium takes its name from Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia, where Karl Ernst Claus isolated it in 1844.

45.fact: Rhodium is one of the rarest precious metals, and most of it ends up in the catalytic converters that clean car exhaust.

46.fact: Palladium takes up hydrogen so readily that it is used to purify hydrogen gas, and it was central to the cold fusion experiments of the late 1980s.

47.fact: Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal and reflects light better too.

48.fact: Cadmium was discovered in 1817 as an impurity in a zinc compound and was long used in rechargeable nickel-cadmium batteries.

49.fact: Indium is soft enough to cut with a knife, and a bar of it makes a high-pitched cry when it is bent.

50.fact: Mixing tin with copper makes bronze, the alloy that gave the Bronze Age its name.

51.fact: Powdered antimony compounds have been used as cosmetics since ancient times, often as the dark eye make-up known as kohl.

52.fact: Taking in even tiny amounts of tellurium can give people breath that smells strongly of garlic.

53.fact: Iodine is a shiny dark solid that melts into a deep violet liquid and boils into a violet gas, and its name comes from the Greek for violet.

54.fact: Xenon is the fuel of ion engines that have pushed spacecraft such as NASA's Dawn probe through space.

55.fact: The second is defined by caesium: it is exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation from a caesium-133 atom.

56.fact: Barium sulfate blocks X-rays, so since 1908 doctors have used it to make the digestive system show up on X-ray images.

57.fact: Lanthanum gives its name to the whole lanthanide series, and its oxide is used to make high-quality camera lenses.

58.fact: Cerium metal catches fire so easily that it is used in ferrocerium lighters, and cerium oxide is used to polish glass.

59.fact: Praseodymium was split in 1885 out of didymium, a mixture once thought to be one element, and the pure metal slowly grows a green coating in air.

60.fact: Neodymium magnets are the strongest widely available permanent magnets, used in audio equipment, hard disk drives and electric car motors.

61.fact: Promethium is named after Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire for humans, and it is radioactive although both its neighbours are stable.

62.fact: Samarium was the first element named, indirectly, after a person: the mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets.

63.fact: Red-glowing security marks on euro banknotes are made with europium, which helps to spot forgeries.

64.fact: Gadolinium compounds are injected into patients as contrast agents to make MRI scans clearer.

65.fact: Most of the world's terbium goes into green phosphors, which gave the green glow of fluorescent lamps and old television tubes.

66.fact: Dysprosium's name comes from the Greek word for hard to get, because it was so difficult to separate from other elements.

67.fact: Holmium has the highest magnetic permeability of any element, so it is used for the pole pieces of the strongest static magnets.

68.fact: Erbium gives glass a pink tint, and glass fibres doped with erbium amplify the light signals sent through optical cables.

69.fact: Thulium is named after Thule, an ancient name for a far northern land, and it is the second-least abundant lanthanide in Earth's crust.

70.fact: Ytterbium atoms tick inside some of the most precise atomic clocks ever built.

71.fact: Lutetium is named after Lutetia, the Latin name for Paris.

72.fact: Hafnium is named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where it was discovered.

73.fact: Tantalum was named after Tantalus, who in Greek myth could never drink the water around him, because the metal cannot soak up acid.

74.fact: Tungsten melts at about 3,422 °C, the highest of any metal, and its symbol W comes from its other name, wolfram.

75.fact: Rhenium, found in 1925, was the last element with a stable isotope to be discovered.

76.fact: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, about twice as dense as lead.

77.fact: A worldwide layer of rock rich in iridium helped show that an asteroid struck Earth when the dinosaurs died out.

78.fact: Until 2019 the kilogram was defined by a single cylinder of platinum and iridium alloy, made in 1879.

79.fact: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet of about one square metre.

80.fact: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

81.fact: Thallium was discovered in 1861 from a bright green line in its spectrum, and its name comes from the Greek for green shoot.

82.fact: Lead's symbol Pb comes from its Latin name, plumbum, and lead production in Roman times reached unprecedented levels.

83.fact: Bismuth crystals grow in stair-step shapes, and a thin layer of oxide makes them shimmer with rainbow colours.

84.fact: Polonium was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898 and named after Marie's homeland, Poland.

85.fact: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust: less than a gram of it exists at any one time.

86.fact: Radon is a radioactive gas that is denser than air, so it can collect in basements and crawl spaces under homes.

87.fact: Francium, found by Marguerite Perey in 1939, was the last element discovered in nature rather than made in a lab.

88.fact: Radium's radiation makes some chemicals glow, so after its discovery it was widely used in paints that shine in the dark.

89.fact: Actinium is so radioactive that it glows with a pale blue light in the dark.

90.fact: Thorium is named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder, and is about three times as abundant in Earth's crust as uranium.

91.fact: Protactinium's name means precursor of actinium, because it decays into actinium.

92.fact: Uranium was named after the planet Uranus, which had been discovered only eight years earlier.

93.fact: Neptunium, the first element heavier than uranium to be made, was named after Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus.

94.fact: The heat from decaying plutonium-238 has powered spacecraft such as the Voyager probes and the Curiosity rover.

95.fact: Many household smoke detectors contain a tiny amount of americium.

96.fact: Curium, named after Marie and Pierre Curie, has been the radiation source in instruments that analyse rocks on Mars.

97.fact: Berkelium is named after Berkeley, California, where it was first made in 1949.

98.fact: Californium gives off so many neutrons that tiny amounts are used to start up nuclear reactors.

99.fact: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test, in 1952, and is named after Albert Einstein.

100.fact: Fermium was found in the debris of the same 1952 hydrogen bomb test as einsteinium and is named after Enrico Fermi.

101.fact: Mendelevium is named after Dmitri Mendeleev, and the first experiment to make it produced only 17 atoms.

102.fact: Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite who founded the Nobel Prizes.

103.fact: Lawrencium is named after Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron, a machine that speeds up particles.

104.fact: Rutherfordium, named after physicist Ernest Rutherford, is not found in nature and can only be made in a particle accelerator.

105.fact: Dubnium is named after Dubna, the Russian town that is home to the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research.

106.fact: Seaborgium honours the chemist Glenn T. Seaborg, who was still alive when the name was chosen.

107.fact: Bohrium is named after Niels Bohr, whose model of the atom inspired diagrams like the one on this page.

108.fact: Hassium is named after Hesse, the German state where it was first made in 1984.

109.fact: Meitnerium honours Lise Meitner, one of the discoverers of nuclear fission.

110.fact: Darmstadtium is named after the German city of Darmstadt, where it was first made in 1994.

111.fact: Roentgenium is named after Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays.

112.fact: Copernicium honours the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, and its name was made official on the 537th anniversary of his birth.

113.fact: Nihonium was the first element named by a team in Asia, and its name comes from Nihon, a Japanese name for Japan.

114.fact: Flerovium is named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, where it was first made.

115.fact: Moscovium is named after the Moscow region, home to the laboratory in Dubna where it was first made.

116.fact: Livermorium is named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, and only about 35 atoms of it had been made by 2020.

117.fact: Tennessine is named after the US state of Tennessee, home to Oak Ridge National Laboratory and other research centres.

118.fact: Oganesson, the heaviest known element, honours Yuri Oganessian, who played a leading role in discovering the heaviest elements.
